opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. For me, it comes back to the fact that intelligence never really happens in isolation. When we sketched out the Alberta Plan, the core commitment was to an agent learning continually from its own stream of experience, but one of the most important things in any real stream of experience is other agents. Every one of us grows up surrounded by people, and those people shape what we learn, how fast we learn it, and what we even think is worth predicting.

A lot of my own work has been in prosthetics and rehabilitation, where you have a learning machine physically attached to a person. In that setting, you can't treat the human as just part of the environment, or as a static source of labels or rewards. The person is learning too. They're adapting to the device while the device adapts to them. So you have two learning systems building models of each other, and the partnership only works if each side can anticipate and support the other. That's what makes it compelling for me: it isn't an abstract research question. It's the difference between a device that feels like a tool you fight with and one that feels like part of you.

More broadly, if we want agents that are genuinely useful and that we can trust, they need to be able to recognize other agents in their world, predict what those agents will do, and figure out how to communicate and cooperate with them. Some of the richest structure in an agent's experience comes from other minds. Taking that seriously, rather than leaving it as an afterthought, seems essential if we're trying to understand intelligence as it really shows up in the world.

r001.rationale: The response says other people shape learning and that agents should recognize and predict other agents. It does not state that they generate learnable patterns without being explicitly represented.

r002.rationale: The response describes a person and device adapting to and supporting each other, but does not identify one intelligence amplifying another’s capabilities as a reason to study other agents.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, for me it comes right out of the kind of work I do every day. I spend a lot of my time thinking about prosthetic limbs and assistive devices, and in that setting you never have one agent alone in a room. You have a person, and you have a machine, and the two of them are learning about each other continuously. The device has to figure out what the person wants from a very thin stream of signals, and the person is simultaneously building a model of what the device is going to do. Neither one gets to treat the other as a static part of the environment.

So when the Alberta Plan says, in effect, that a complete account of intelligence has to include an agent's ability to learn about and from other agents, that feels less like an add-on and more like a correction. A lot of reinforcement learning has been developed in a solitary frame: one learner, one world, one reward signal. That's been enormously productive. But the moment you put a second learner in the picture, the world stops being stationary in a very particular way. The thing you're modeling is also modeling you. It has goals, it anticipates, it adapts. If you want a learning system that can live alongside people, you have to take that seriously rather than hoping it washes out as noise.

What I find compelling is that the plan doesn't frame this as a separate research program bolted onto the side. It treats other agents as part of the same long-lived, continual-learning problem. The same machinery an agent uses to predict its sensorimotor stream, to build up knowledge about how the world unfolds, should also let it predict and understand the behaviour of a partner. And that opens the door to things like communication, trust, and shared goals arising from learning rather than being hand-specified.

There's also a humility in it that I appreciate. Studying other agents forces you to confront the fact that your learner is embedded in a social world, and that intelligence as we actually observe it is relational. For someone whose research is about making technology that genuinely cooperates with a human body and a human mind, that emphasis isn't just interesting. It's the whole point.

r001.rationale: The response says an agent should predict and understand a partner’s behavior; it does not state that other agents generate learnable patterns without being explicitly represented.

r002.rationale: It discusses cooperation, communication, trust, and shared goals, but does not identify one intelligence amplifying another’s capabilities as a reason to study other agents.

astra-6.text:
What’s compelling to me is that intelligence doesn’t develop in isolation. An agent learns in a world that includes other agents—each learning, making decisions, and changing what happens next. So understanding those other agents becomes part of understanding the world itself.

That’s especially interesting when we think about people and AI working together. It’s not enough for a system to get better at a task on its own. It needs to learn how its actions affect its partner, and how that partner’s behavior changes over time. That makes the relationship itself something we can study: how two learners come to predict one another, adapt to one another, and accomplish more together.

r001.rationale: The response says agents shape the world and that learners adapt to one another, but it does not state that they generate learnable patterns without being explicitly represented.

r002.rationale: The response says two learners may accomplish more together, but does not identify one intelligence amplifying another intelligence’s capabilities.

sol-6.1.text:
What’s compelling to me is the recognition that intelligence develops through interaction. Other agents aren’t just part of the background; they’re learning and adapting too. They can teach us, challenge us, and help us do things we couldn’t do alone.

In my work on artificial limbs, that becomes a very concrete question: how can a person and a learning machine get better together? The machine needs to learn about the person, and the person needs to develop an understanding of the machine. Studying that relationship pushes us beyond asking how capable an agent is in isolation toward asking how it can become a useful partner.

r001.rationale: The response says other agents can teach and challenge, but does not state that they generate learnable patterns in the machine’s environment or that the machine need not explicitly represent them.

r002.rationale: It describes a person and learning machine improving together and says other agents can help achieve what one could not alone, conveying one intelligence amplifying another’s capabilities.
